citationText: “ATSC Standard: Signaling, Delivery, Synchronization, and Error Protection,” Doc. A/331:2020, Advanced Television Systems Committee, Washington, DC, Jan. 16, 2020. Although current deployments require multicast gateways as external hardware devices, it is perfectly reasonable to assume that they could be digitized and located inside the customers’ User Agent devices. BBC R&D group’s attempt to digitalize multicast gateway through WebAssembly was halted due to poor browser support for server push cache manipulation.2 Once the browsers and smartphones start introducing support for more loose Push cache manipulation, it might reignite the interest in bringing that idea to life. In a perfect world, the browsers should be capable of multicast QUIC stream reception completely software-based, without any intermediary devices. QUIC can be coupled with advanced forward errorcorrection schemes like fountain or network codes,31 which will effectively enable proactive error correction over the multicast link, further reducing the signaling overhead and even potentially removing the need for the return link and long buffering times due to retransmission, keeping delivery latencies as low as possible. Related to the ATSC 3.0 test-bed in Copenhagen, the result of this project was to better understand the possibilities and benefits of using QUIC instead of UDP as the network transport protocol, independent of the application layer protocols used ecosystem. In an ATSC 3.0 setup, multicast is used in a variety of ways with most transport protocols relying on UDP with error correction, as TCP will only impose the previously described problems. With the use of QUIC, reliability is taken to a new level, and the intention is to use QUIC in the entire chain from ingestion to presentation on the end-user device. The project only followed the distribution of media content using HTTP/3 over QUIC in an infrastructure always relying on two-way communication available in all distribution entities, for example, the CDN scenario. The next step is to integrate QUIC into the IP broadcast ecosystem, using a modified ROUTE protocol over ATSC 3.0 and DVB-GSE as bearer technologies and reaching the gateway. The reliability of QUIC, in the presented implementation, will depend on the broadband available at the gateway. Alternative methods exist, using forward error correction in separate ROUTE repair sessions [13], to carry out stream repair at the gateway without the need for an active internet connection. This is to ensure a reliable reception even at locations with a very poor or no internet connectivity. Preliminary trails have been carried out, and the results will be presented in a separate article. Conclusion In this work, we presented a solution that can serve as the reference architecture for multicast QUICbased enhancement to CDNs, allowing for efficient and secure content distribution of audio–video content using various low-latency techniques for HTTP
